# Abstract

## Structured abstract

Background

High systolic blood pressure and high LDL cholesterol are leading modifiable drivers of cardiovascular disease (CVD) burden worldwide, but the joint impact of achieving WHO targets for hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy has not been quantified.

Methods

We did a comparative risk assessment modelling study using a multi-state transition model for `r n_countries` countries, 2026 - 2050. The model projected deaths from ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, and hypertensive heart disease by age, sex, and country, using WHO Global Health Estimates, GBD 2023, UN World Population Prospects 2024, NCD Risk Factor Collaboration data, and effect estimates. We compared business-as-usual with three intervention scenarios: hypertension control in the general population to reach the WHO target of 150 million people controlled by 2030; 80% blood pressure control among people with diabetes by 2030; 50% statin coverage among eligible adults aged 40 years or older by 2030; and a combined scenario. The primary outcome was cumulative CVD deaths averted during 2026 - 2050.

Findings

Under business-as-usual, the model projected `r fmt_m(bau_total_deaths)` million CVD deaths during 2026 - 2050. Compared with business-as-usual, achieving the general-population hypertension target was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_bp)` million deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_bp)` million DALYs, the diabetes-specific hypertension target `r fmt_m(total_bpd)` million deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_bpd)` million DALYs, and the statin target `r fmt_m(total_stat)` million deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_stat)` million DALYs. Achieving all three targets simultaneously was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_all)` million CVD deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs, equivalent to `r pct_all`% of cumulative business-as-usual mortality.

Interpretation

Achieving WHO targets for blood pressure control and lipid-lowering therapy could yield large and complementary reductions in CVD mortality and disability. The largest absolute gains were projected in middle-income countries and the largest proportional gains in low-income settings. These estimates represent technical potential under assumptions of linear scale-up, full adherence, and no secular change in baseline risk-factor distributions.

Funding

This work is funded by the World Health Organization.

\newpage

## Research in context

Evidence before this study

We searched PubMed and Embase from inception to 31 March 2026 for multi-country modelling studies estimating the mortality impact of hypertension control or lipid-lowering therapy, using search terms combining cardiovascular mortality, blood pressure lowering, statin therapy, global or multi-country modelling, and projection; we supplemented this with reference list review of included studies and of WHO and NCD Countdown 2030 technical reports. The clinical case for both interventions is settled: meta-analyses by Ettehad and colleagues [-@Ettehad2016] and by the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration [@Fulcher2015] provide the trial-based effect sizes on which current WHO treatment guidelines rest. What has remained unquantified is the combined global mortality impact of treating both risk factors simultaneously at scale. Kontis and colleagues [-@Kontis2019] projected that antihypertensive scale-up to 70% coverage could delay up to 39.4 million deaths over 25 years; Pickersgill and colleagues [-@Pickersgill2022] estimated 76--130 million deaths averted under the 80-80-80 hypertension target but did not model statin therapy. The NCD Countdown 2030 analyses identified both interventions as among the most cost-efficient pathways to SDG target 3.4 but did not quantify their joint impact [@Watkins2022NCD2030; @Bennett2020NCD2030Path]. No published study has simultaneously projected the mortality consequences of achieving the 150-million hypertension control target, the Global Diabetes Compact 80% control target for people with diabetes, and the 50% statin coverage target across `r n_countries` countries, evaluated individually and in combination against a common business-as-usual baseline.

Added value of this study

Using a discrete-time multi-state transition model calibrated to GBD 2023, WHO Global Health Estimates, and UNWPP 2024 data, this study estimates that achieving all three WHO targets could avert `r fmt_m(total_all)` million CVD deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs across `r n_countries` countries from 2026 to 2050. These projections assume full adherence, linear scale-up to 2030, and no secular change in baseline risk-factor distributions --- assumptions that define a technical ceiling rather than a likely outcome. The model credits only coverage increments above country-specific baselines to avoid double-counting existing treatment benefits and combines intervention effects multiplicatively to reflect the partial independence of blood pressure and lipid-lowering pathways. Disaggregation by cause of death, age, sex, WHO region, and World Bank income group allows direct comparison of where the health gains are largest and for whom they accrue.

Implications of all the available evidence

Trial evidence, prior global modelling, and the present projections consistently point in the same direction: blood pressure control and statin therapy are complementary, not competing, priorities, and the health gains from pursuing both together exceed what either achieves alone. The largest absolute benefits fall in lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income countries; the largest proportional gains are in low-income countries and the African region, where the distance between current coverage and the WHO targets is greatest --- and where the cost of inaction compounds year by year. How much of this projected ceiling is reachable in practice will depend on health system capacity, drug supply, and whether the political commitments made at the 2025 UN High-level Meeting on NCDs are matched by sustained financing and implementation support.

\newpage

# Introduction
Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the world's leading cause of death and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) [@Mensah2023GlobalBurdenCVD; @Chong2024]. CVD deaths increased globally from 13.1 million in 1990 to 19.2 million in 2023, with ischaemic heart disease, intracerebral haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic stroke, and hypertensive heart disease among the leading causes [@GBDCVD2025]. Age-standardized CVD DALY rates were highest in low and low-middle Socio-demographic Index (SDI) settings, and the number of prevalent CVD cases more than doubled between 1990 and 2023, rising from 311 million to 626 million [@GBDCVD2025]. In 2023, modifiable risk factors accounted for 79.6% of CVD burden, equivalent to 347 million DALYs --- underscoring that the majority of this burden is preventable [@Chong2024; @Agboyibor2025CVHWHOAfrica].

Among modifiable exposures, high systolic blood pressure and high low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol rank as the two leading contributors to attributable CVD burden worldwide, together accounting for a greater share of ischaemic heart disease and stroke mortality than dietary risks, air pollution, or any other single risk factor [@Geldsetzer2019HypertensionCareLMICs; @ConsortiumRisk2023]. The scale of unmet need is striking: 1.4 billion adults live with high blood pressure, yet only 23% have it under control [@WHO2025HypertensionReport]. The estimated global prevalence of hypercholesterolaemia was 24.1% in 2025, and that of hypertriglyceridaemia 28.8%, with statin therapy coverage remaining far below levels needed for meaningful population-level risk reduction [@Marcus2022StatinsLMICs]. Beyond their magnitude of effect, blood pressure control and lipid-lowering therapy are distinguished by the availability of effective, affordable, and scalable pharmaceutical interventions and established primary health care delivery platforms --- making them implementation priorities of the highest order [@Agboyibor2025CVHWHOAfrica].

Multiple multilateral frameworks now reflect convergent political commitment to tackling these two risk factors as a cornerstone of NCD prevention. WHO Member States have endorsed progressively ambitious targets: the 2021 Global Diabetes Compact committed to 80% blood pressure control and systematic statin therapy for all adults aged 40 years and above with diabetes [@Hunt2021GlobalDiabetesCompact; @Gregg2023DiabetesCompactTargets]. The WHO NCD Global Monitoring Framework set a target of at least 50% of eligible high-risk individuals receiving effective drug therapies, including statins, by 2025 [@WHO2011NCDMonitoringFramework]; and the Political Declaration of the Fourth High-level Meeting on NCDs (2025) called for 80% of primary health care facilities to stock WHO-recommended essential medicines by 2030, alongside control of blood pressure in an additional 150 million people. The present study quantifies what achieving these targets would mean in practice --- in health and economic terms, across `r n_countries` countries.

Although the clinical benefits of these interventions are well established, comparable global evidence quantifying the long-term mortality, morbidity, and economic returns of simultaneously achieving both targets across the full spectrum of country income levels remains limited. Existing analyses have typically been restricted to single countries, short time horizons, or individual interventions modelled in isolation, constraining the ability of national governments, international donors, and health institutions to prioritise investment and plan implementation at scale.

This study addresses that gap by estimating the health and economic outcomes associated with achieving WHO targets for hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy across `r n_countries` countries from 2026 to 2050, using a comparative risk assessment modelling framework applied to country-specific epidemiological and demographic data.

# Methods

## Study design

We conducted a multi-country comparative modelling study using a discrete-time multi-state transition model projecting CVD mortality across `r n_countries` countries from 2026 to 2050. Four causes of CVD death were modelled jointly: ischaemic heart disease (IHD), ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage (haemorrhagic stroke), and hypertensive heart disease. Three health states --- Well, Sick, and Dead --- were tracked for each cause, stratified by single year of age (20--95), sex, and country. The model was calibrated to observed epidemiological data from 2019 and projected forward using annual time steps (see Multi-State Transition Model). The model structure and intervention framework were informed by prior global modelling and implementation evidence, including the Global 80-80-80 hypertension control targets [@Pickersgill2022], and the budget impact of the WHO HEARTS technical package for cardiovascular disease management [@Garcia2026HEARTS4Countries].

## Data sources

Death counts and mortality rates were derived from the World Health Organization Global Health Estimates (GHE). Prevalence estimates were obtained from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 study. Population denominators were taken from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 revision, using single-year age- and sex-specific projections for each country. Blood pressure distributions were sourced from the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, and baseline hypertension control rates were based on country-level analyses provided by WHO. Relative risks for blood pressure reduction were based on the meta-analysis by Ettehad et al. [-@Ettehad2016], stratified by blood pressure category and cause. COVID-19 excess mortality was applied only to 2020--2021. Statin coverage estimates were derived from published and imputed country-level data, with intervention effect sizes drawn from established randomised controlled trial evidence [@Fulcher2015].


## Intervention scenarios

Three active intervention scenarios were modelled against a business-as-usual (BAU) reference in which 2024 coverage rates were held constant through 2050:

1. **Hypertension control (general population):** Linear scale-up of population-level blood pressure control by 2030, beginning in 2026, corresponding to the WHO target of 150 million additional people with controlled hypertension. Effect sizes were derived from the Ettehad et al. meta-analysis, applied across eight blood pressure bins with incremental coverage above baseline generating new risk reductions for incidence and case fatality (see Hypertension Control Intervention Model).

2. **Hypertension control (diabetes subgroup):** Linear scale-up to 80% blood pressure control among people with diagnosed diabetes by 2030. Effect sizes were weighted by country-level diabetes prevalence and blended with general-population hypertension effects (see Hypertension Control Intervention Model: Diabetes Component).

3. **Lipid-lowering therapy:** Linear scale-up to 50% statin coverage among eligible adults (aged 40 years and older) by 2030. Effects were restricted to IHD and ischaemic stroke and applied through an attributable-fraction approach, with an atherosclerotic fraction of 0.60 for ischaemic stroke (see Statin Therapy Intervention Model).

A fourth combination scenario applied all three interventions simultaneously, with effects combining multiplicatively across interventions (see Multi-State Transition Model).

## Modelling framework

The core model is a discrete-time state-transition framework in which individuals move between Well, Sick, and Dead states at each annual time step according to cause-specific incidence rates (Well to Sick), case fatality rates (Sick to Dead), and background mortality rates (all states to Dead). Interventions modify incidence and case fatality through multiplicative effect ratios ($\varepsilon_{IR}$, $\varepsilon_{CF}$), which are computed from the intervention-specific coverage increment above baseline. Only incremental coverage above baseline was credited with new effects, avoiding double-counting of existing treatment benefits. For hypertension control, effect ratios are derived from a nine-step pipeline incorporating blood pressure bin distributions, GBD relative risks, Ettehad trial effect sizes, and population-weighted aggregation. For statin therapy, incremental coverage generates cause- and location-specific risk reductions applied to incidence and case fatality. Under the combined scenario, effects combine multiplicatively: $\varepsilon_{IR,\text{total}} = \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}} \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{statin}}$ (see Mathematical Notation Summary).

## Calibration

Incidence (IR) and case fatality (CF) parameters were calibrated jointly to ensure consistency with external data sources: incidence rates were adjusted to reproduce age-, sex-, country-, and cause-specific incidence patterns from GBD 2023, while case-fatality parameters were calibrated to match observed cause-specific mortality counts from WHO GHE within each stratum. COVID-19 excess mortality was incorporated for 2020–2021 only (see Key Parameter Appendix).


## Data and code availability

All input data used in this analysis are publicly available from their original sources (e.g., WHO Global Health Estimates). Processed inputs and model code are provided in the project repository: https://github.com/Disease-Control-Priorities/uw-who-cvdtargets. Model outputs (results) can be accessed and downloaded at the same link. All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.1), and full scripts are openly available in the repository.


## Outcomes

The primary outcome was cumulative CVD deaths averted relative to the BAU scenario over 2026--2050, disaggregated by intervention, cause of death, age group, sex, WHO region, and World Bank income group. Secondary outcomes included years of life lost (YLLs) averted, years lived with disability (YLDs) averted, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) averted.

Burden of disease was quantified using three complementary metrics: years of life lost (YLL), years lived with disability (YLD), and disability-adjusted life years (DALY), where $DALY = YLL + YLD$. Remaining life expectancy at each age of death was obtained from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 revision (medium variant), providing country- and year-specific values. Disability weights were derived from GBD 2023 data as the ratio of cause-specific YLDs to prevalence for each cause and location. No age weighting or time discounting was applied; all estimates are undiscounted (see Supplemental Material: DALY Calculation Methods).

## Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis

The model was run under the primary set of assumptions described above. Formal probabilistic sensitivity analysis incorporating GBD uncertainty intervals and parameter distributions is planned as a subsequent extension. The present analysis reports central estimates derived from mean input parameters.

## Economic valuation {#sec:econ-methods}

<!-- The economic value of averted CVD mortality was estimated using two complementary metrics: the value of a statistical life (VSL) and the value of a statistical life year (VSLY). Both metrics quantify the monetary value that society places on small reductions in mortality risk and are recommended by guidelines for benefit--cost analysis of health interventions [@Robinson2019VSL]. -->

The economic value of averted CVD mortality was estimated using the value of a statistical life year (VSLY). This metric quantifies the monetary value that society places on marginal reductions in mortality risk and is recommended in guidelines for benefit–cost analyses of health interventions, particularly those targeting age-specific populations such as adults [@Robinson2019VSL; @Robinson19BCA].

Country-specific VSLY values were derived by transferring a United States reference VSL to each country using gross national income (GNI) per capita at purchasing power parity (PPP) and an income elasticity. Following Robinson et al. [-@Robinson2019VSL], the primary estimate used a differential income elasticity of 0.8 for countries at or above US income and 1.2 for countries below. A uniform elasticity of 1.5 was used as a sensitivity bound. GNI per capita was obtained from the World Bank and projected beyond the last observed year using SSP2 GDP growth rates from IIASA SSP 3.1 [@IIASA2024Gdp31].

The constant VSLY was derived as $\text{VSLY} = \text{VSL} / e_{\bar{a}}$, where $e_{\bar{a}}$ is the undiscounted remaining life expectancy at the population-weighted average adult age. The monetary value of averted mortality in each country-year was then computed as the product of the VSLY and the total undiscounted life-years gained, where life-years gained were calculated as $\sum_a \text{deaths averted}(a) \times e_x(a)$, with $e_x(a)$ being the remaining life expectancy at the age of death from UNWPP 2024.

Annual monetary values were discounted to 2026 present value at a calendar-year discount rate of 3%. Results are presented as cumulative present values and as a proportion of discounted national income (population $\times$ GNI per capita) to facilitate cross-country comparison. A similar reporting approach has been used in prior studies [@Verguet2024ECValue;@Chang2024ECValue]. Full mathematical details are provided in the Supplemental Material (see Economic Valuation Methods).

# Results

## Baseline global trajectory, 2026--2050

Under the business-as-usual (BAU) scenario, in which hypertension control and statin coverage remained at 2024 levels, the model projected `r fmt_m(bau_total_deaths)` million cumulative CVD deaths from the four modelled causes across `r n_countries` countries during 2026--2050 (Supplemental Figure S1). Ischaemic heart disease accounted for the largest share of deaths, followed by ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, and hypertensive heart disease. Incident and prevalent CVD cases were projected to increase throughout the study period, driven largely by population ageing. Although age-standardised CVD mortality rates declined modestly under BAU, the absolute number of deaths increased because population growth and ageing outpaced reductions in age-specific mortality rates.

## Global impact of achieving the hypertension control target

Achievement of the WHO target for hypertension control in the general population was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_bp)` million CVD deaths during `r study_years`, equivalent to `r pct_bp`% of cumulative BAU mortality (Table 1; Supplemental Figure S2). The annual number of deaths averted increased steadily from the start of scale-up in 2026, reaching `r fmt_k(annual_2030_bp)` thousand in 2030 and `r fmt_k(annual_2050_bp)` thousand in 2050, reflecting the cumulative benefit of sustained blood pressure control over time (Supplemental Figure S3). Benefits were observed across all four CVD causes, with the largest absolute reductions in ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke, followed by intracerebral haemorrhage and hypertensive heart disease (Table 2). Over the full study period, general-population hypertension control was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_dalys_bp)` million DALYs.

Targeted hypertension control among people with diabetes, assuming scale-up to 80% control by 2030, was projected to avert a further `r fmt_m(total_bpd)` million deaths, corresponding to `r pct_bpd`% of cumulative BAU mortality, and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_bpd)` million DALYs during `r study_years`. These gains reflect the higher underlying cardiovascular risk in this subgroup and the greater absolute benefit associated with improved blood pressure control.

## Global impact of achieving the lipid-lowering therapy target

Scale-up of lipid-lowering therapy to 50% coverage among eligible adults by 2030 was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_stat)` million deaths during `r study_years`, equivalent to `r pct_stat`% of cumulative BAU mortality (Table 1). Because statin effects were restricted to ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke, the distribution of averted deaths differed from that in the hypertension scenarios: `r fmt_m(averted_ihd_stat)` million deaths averted were attributable to reductions in ischaemic heart disease and `r fmt_m(averted_istroke_stat)` million to reductions in ischaemic stroke (Table 2). The temporal pattern of benefit was similar to that of hypertension control, with gains increasing after 2030 as sustained treatment coverage translated into cumulative reductions in cardiovascular risk (Supplemental Figure S3). Overall, lipid-lowering therapy was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_dalys_stat)` million DALYs over the study period.

## Combined impact of both targets

Simultaneous achievement of all three WHO targets was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_all)` million CVD deaths during `r study_years`, representing `r pct_all`% of cumulative BAU mortality (Table 1; Supplemental Figure S2). The combined scenario yielded greater benefit than any single intervention alone, consistent with the complementary effects of hypertension control and statin therapy acting through partially overlapping but distinct causal pathways. By 2050, the combined scenario was projected to avert approximately `r fmt_k(annual_2050_all)` thousand deaths annually relative to BAU (Figure 1). Across the full study period, it was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs, comprising `r fmt_m(total_ylls_all)` million YLLs and `r fmt_m(total_ylds_all)` million YLDs (Table 3).

Under the combined scenario, ischaemic heart disease accounted for the largest number of deaths averted (`r fmt_m(averted_ihd_all)` million), followed by intracerebral haemorrhage (`r fmt_m(averted_hstroke_all)` million), ischaemic stroke (`r fmt_m(averted_istroke_all)` million), and hypertensive heart disease (`r fmt_m(averted_hhd_all)` million; Table 2).

## Heterogeneity across countries and regions

Projected health gains varied across WHO regions. These differences reflected the combined influence of population size, baseline CVD burden, and treatment coverage gaps, with the largest proportional reductions in regions characterised by high hypertension prevalence and low baseline treatment coverage (Figure 3; Table 4).

When stratified by World Bank income group, low-income and lower-middle-income countries together accounted for a substantial share of avertable deaths and DALYs, underscoring the equity implications of achieving these global targets (Table 5). Upper-middle-income countries, which include several of the world's most populous countries, contributed the largest absolute number of deaths and DALYs averted. High-income countries showed smaller proportional gains, consistent with higher baseline levels of hypertension control and statin coverage.

## Distribution by age and sex

The projected benefits of all interventions were concentrated in older adults. Under the combined scenario, adults aged 70 years and older accounted for `r fmt_m(averted_70_79 + averted_80_89 + averted_90p)` million of the `r fmt_m(total_all)` million deaths averted, reflecting the steep increase in CVD mortality with age (Figure 2). Adults younger than 70 years accounted for `r fmt_m(averted_lt70)` million deaths averted, indicating a substantial reduction in premature CVD mortality, consistent with SDG target 3.4.

Males accounted for `r fmt_m(averted_male)` million averted deaths and females for `r fmt_m(averted_female)` million, consistent with higher age-specific CVD mortality rates in males. The relative contributions of hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy were broadly similar in both sexes, although the absolute number of deaths averted was greater among males across all intervention scenarios (Figure 2).

The relevance of these intervention strategies extends beyond aggregate mortality reduction to the prevention of premature death among working-age populations. Of the `r fmt_m(total_all)` million deaths averted under the combined scenario, `r fmt_m(averted_lt70)` million occurred among adults younger than 70 years --- the age threshold used by SDG target 3.4 to define premature NCD mortality. This concentration of avertable deaths in younger age groups reflects both the high incidence of acute cardiovascular events in mid-life, particularly among males (`r fmt_m(averted_male)` million averted deaths in males versus `r fmt_m(averted_female)` million in females), and the large treatment coverage gaps that persist in the age groups most affected by untreated hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Preventing these deaths has implications that reach beyond the health sector: premature CVD mortality removes economically active individuals from the labour force, reduces household income, and imposes caregiving burdens on surviving family members, with disproportionate consequences in low-income and lower-middle-income countries where social protection systems are weakest. The finding that a substantial fraction of avertable deaths falls within working-age populations strengthens the economic and equity case for accelerated scale-up of both hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy.

## Economic outcomes {#sec:econ-results}

Globally, the economic value of avoided CVD mortality from all interventions between 2026 and 2050 is equivalent to `r fmt_pct_income(econ_scalars$world_vsly_share_total)` of annual income, amounting to a cumulative value of US$`r fmt_t(econ_scalars$world_vsly_value_total)` trillion (discounted at 3% using the value of a statistical life year approach; Table 6; Supplemental Figure S8).

## Sensitivity and uncertainty results

This analysis reports central estimates based on mean input parameters from GBD 2023, meta-analytic treatment effect estimates, and assumptions of linear intervention scale-up. Formal probabilistic sensitivity analyses incorporating uncertainty in epidemiological inputs and intervention effects are planned in subsequent work. These findings should therefore be interpreted as central scenario estimates under the main model assumptions.

# Discussion

## Principal findings

In this study, simultaneous achievement of the three WHO cardiovascular risk-factor targets across `r n_countries` countries between 2026 and 2050 was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_all)` million CVD deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs, equivalent to `r pct_all`% of cumulative business-as-usual mortality. Of the three interventions, hypertension control in the general population produced the largest single effect, averting `r fmt_m(total_bp)` million deaths (`r pct_bp`% of BAU mortality). This finding likely reflects both the broad causal role of elevated blood pressure across all four modelled CVD outcomes and the large unmet need for hypertension treatment and control, particularly in low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Lipid-lowering therapy was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_stat)` million deaths (`r pct_stat`%), with benefits concentrated mainly in ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke, in keeping with the more specific pathway through which LDL cholesterol lowering reduces cardiovascular risk. Targeted hypertension control among people with diabetes was projected to avert a further `r fmt_m(total_bpd)` million deaths (`r pct_bpd`%), a substantial effect relative to the size of this population, consistent with their high underlying cardiovascular risk. Importantly, the combined scenario produced greater benefit than would be expected from simply adding the individual intervention effects. This pattern is consistent with blood pressure control and statin therapy acting through partly independent pathways, so that each intervention reduces some of the residual risk left after the others are applied. Taken together, these findings suggest that pursuing both intervention types in parallel is likely to yield larger health gains than prioritising either strategy alone.

## Interpretation of hypertension control findings

The primacy of hypertension control in our projections --- `r fmt_m(total_bp)` million deaths averted from the general-population intervention alone, rising to `r fmt_m(total_bp + total_bpd)` million when the diabetes-specific target is added --- reflects a straightforward epidemiological reality: raised systolic blood pressure is the single largest attributable risk factor for CVD mortality globally [@Vollset2024], it acts across four mechanistically distinct disease pathways simultaneously, and the gap between where most countries stand today and where the WHO target requires them to be remains vast. As of 2024, approximately 1.4 billion adults were living with hypertension worldwide, yet fewer than one in four had the condition adequately controlled, and in 99 countries national control rates remain below 20% [@WHO2025HypertensionReport]. The progressive annual trajectory of benefit we project --- `r fmt_k(annual_2030_bp)` thousand deaths averted per year by 2030, growing to `r fmt_k(annual_2050_bp)` thousand by 2050 --- reflects the compounding logic of sustained coverage: every year of treatment prevents incident events and simultaneously builds a population with lower cumulative exposure to elevated pressure, reducing case fatality in those who already live with disease. The finding is consistent with the 80-80-80 modelling by Pickersgill and colleagues [-@Pickersgill2022], who estimated 76--130 million all-cause deaths averted over a comparable projection period under full hypertension cascade achievement --- a broader target than the 150-million-person WHO control goal modelled here.

The additional `r fmt_m(total_bpd)` million deaths averted from targeted control among people with diabetes reflects the well-established amplification of cardiovascular risk in this subgroup: diabetes exacerbates endothelial dysfunction, accelerates atherosclerosis, and clusters with hypertension and dyslipidaemia in ways that make each risk factor more dangerous than it would be in isolation [@ADAPP2025StandardsDiabetesCVD]. A cross-sectional study of 38 low-income and middle-income countries found that fewer than half of people with diagnosed diabetes had achieved blood pressure targets [@Moran2023GlobalHEARTSImplementation], and fewer than one in ten were using statins [@Li2024DiabetesCVDTargetsLMICs] --- figures that illustrate how far current practice in many settings lies from the 80% control standard demanded by the Global Diabetes Compact [@Gregg2023DiabetesCompactTargets]. Reaching that standard does not require novel technologies; it requires the same primary-care building blocks --- standardised treatment protocols, reliable drug supply, team-based follow-up --- that the HEARTS technical package has already demonstrated are implementable at scale in more than 40 low-income and middle-income countries [@Garcia2026HEARTS4Countries; @Banigbe2025].

## Interpretation of lipid-lowering therapy findings

The projection that statin scale-up to 50% coverage could avert `r fmt_m(total_stat)` million CVD deaths over 2026--2050 deserves to be read alongside one uncomfortable fact: across 41 low-income and middle-income countries, statin use among those eligible for primary prevention was approximately 8%, and for secondary prevention approximately 22% --- and the WHO 50% coverage target was not achieved by a single income group, region, or, with one exception, country [@Marcus2022StatinsLMICs]. The intervention modelled here is therefore not an incremental improvement on a system approaching its target; it is a near-doubling of coverage starting from a very low base in most of the world. The `r fmt_m(averted_ihd_stat)` million deaths averted from ischaemic heart disease --- which accounts for nearly all of the statin effect --- reflects both the high atherosclerotic fraction of IHD burden globally and the size of the absolute risk reduction achievable from LDL cholesterol lowering in populations with currently near-zero treatment rates. The asymmetry between IHD and ischaemic stroke estimates --- `r fmt_m(averted_ihd_stat)` million versus `r fmt_m(averted_istroke_stat)` million --- is mechanistically expected: the atherosclerotic fraction of ischaemic stroke that is sensitive to statin therapy is substantially smaller than for IHD, and we applied this restriction through a 0.60 atherosclerotic proportion for ischaemic stroke case fatality, consistent with established estimates [@Petty1999IschemicStrokeSubtypes]. The fact that statin therapy nonetheless contributes `r pct_stat`% of business-as-usual mortality averted despite this mechanistic constraint strengthens the argument for treating lipid-lowering access as a standalone NCD priority rather than a residual consideration after blood pressure programmes are in place. The barriers are not ones of clinical uncertainty --- the evidence from the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration is among the most robust in preventive medicine [@Reith2026StatinAdverseEffects] --- but structural: irregular drug supply, absence of lipid testing at primary care level, provider unfamiliarity with simplified prescribing protocols, and out-of-pocket costs that make long-term adherence inaccessible for many patients in resource-constrained settings [@Marcus2022StatinsLMICs; @Li2024HyperlipidemiaMedicinesAccess; @Fulcher2015].

## Combined policy meaning

The most consequential finding in this study may not be the headline total but the structure beneath it. The combined scenario averted more than the sum of its parts not because the effects happened to overlap neatly, but because blood pressure control and LDL cholesterol lowering act through genuinely different pathways to CVD harm. Raised systolic pressure injures the endothelium, stiffens arterial walls, and drives haemodynamic stress across all vascular beds; elevated LDL drives lipid deposition and atherosclerotic plaque progression, predominantly in coronary and cerebrovascular territories. Each intervention therefore reaches risk that the other leaves largely untouched, and the multiplicative combination we modelled reflects that biological reality (see Multi-State Transition Model). This independence is well established in randomised trial evidence and underpins the integrated antihypertensive-plus-statin protocols that Moran and colleagues have designed specifically for primary care delivery in low-income and middle-income countries --- protocols that allow a non-physician health worker to initiate both treatments in a single clinic visit, without waiting for lipid laboratory results, using age, diabetes status, and blood pressure level as eligibility criteria [@Moran2024; @Watkins2022NCD2030].

The practical implication of multiplicative independence is that concentrating investment in either hypertension control or statin therapy, while treating the other as a future priority, surrenders preventable deaths that only the deferred intervention would have reached. The SECURE trial demonstrated that a polypill combining an antihypertensive with atorvastatin improved adherence and reduced major cardiovascular events by 24% relative to usual care among post-myocardial infarction patients --- direct clinical evidence that co-delivery is not only biologically justified but practically achievable [@Castellano2022PolypillSecondaryPrevention]. The cardiovascular polypill, added to the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines in 2023 as a fixed-dose combination of antihypertensive and statin therapy, extends this delivery logic to primary prevention, with cost-effectiveness analyses from low-income and middle-income country settings reporting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios well below conventional willingness-to-pay thresholds [@KohliLynch2025PolypillCostEffectiveness]. The convergence of the HEARTS operational framework, the integrated protocol evidence, the polypill's inclusion on the essential medicines list, and the multiplicative biology of combined risk-factor reduction collectively make the case that these are not two programmes to be sequenced but one patient-centred encounter, engineered to happen at the same moment, at the same primary care facility, for the same person.

## Equity and implementation implications

The global totals in this study risk obscuring the story that matters most. The African region shows the highest proportional benefit under the combined scenario, and low-income countries overall stand to gain disproportionately relative to their share of baseline burden. The gradient runs exactly where you would expect it --- the populations furthest from the WHO targets today are the ones who gain most when those targets are reached. CVD deaths in low-income countries are projected to nearly double by mid-century under business-as-usual trajectories [@Chong2024], driven by population ageing, unchecked hypertension [@Nambiema2025HypertensionAfrica], and statin coverage that remains below 10% for primary prevention in most of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia [@Marcus2022StatinsLMICs]. The WHO's 2025 global hypertension report found that while 93% of high-income countries report availability of the four core antihypertensive drug classes, only 28% of low-income countries do --- and that is before the additional barriers of procurement delays, out-of-pocket costs, and health worker capacity are considered [@WHO2025HypertensionReport]. Our model, which assumes full adherence and linear scale-up to 2030, cannot capture these realities. Its projections define a ceiling, not a forecast, and the distance between that ceiling and what current health system trajectories will actually deliver is itself a measure of the equity gap.

Closing that gap requires strong financing mechanisms, and also the kind of operational infrastructure that HEARTS has shown is achievable in resource-constrained settings: standardised treatment protocols that reduce clinical decision-making to a manageable algorithm, reliable drug supply chains that stock both antihypertensives and generic statins at the primary care level, team-based care models that allow task-sharing to non-physician providers, and information systems that track patients across visits and flag those lost to follow-up. By 2024, more than 22 million people with hypertension were being managed through HEARTS-based programmes in 34 low-income and middle-income countries --- a proof of concept that the model works at scale, and that the primary bottleneck is now coverage rather than design [@Moran2023GlobalHEARTSImplementation; @Banigbe2025]. Expanding HEARTS to include integrated statin prescribing would extend the same infrastructure to lipid-lowering therapy without requiring a parallel programme, a separate supply chain, or additional clinic visits.

The NCD Countdown 2030 estimated that closing the gap would require an additional US$18 billion annually through 2030 --- an amount that would yield a net economic return of US$2.7 trillion and avert 39 million premature deaths across all NCDs [@Watkins2022NCD2030; @Bennett2020NCD2030Path]. Cardiovascular interventions, including hypertension management and statin therapy, sit among the most cost-efficient components of that package [@Agboyibor2025CVHWHOAfrica; @Garcia2026HEARTS4Countries; @Banigbe2025]. Three political declarations since 2011 have come and gone without shifting the trajectory of CVD mortality in the countries that carry the greatest burden [@Lancet2025TurnTideNCDs]. The 2025 declaration carries the same risk. Whether it produces a different outcome will depend not on the language of the text but on whether the resource flows, the supply chain reforms, and the primary care investments it calls for are measurably in place within the next 24 months --- before the window for reaching the 2030 targets closes entirely.

## Economic valuation

The economic valuation reinforces the health case with a fiscal one. Under the combined scenario, the cumulative value of averted CVD mortality over 2026--2050, estimated using the value of a statistical life year approach discounted at 3%, amounted to US$`r fmt_t(econ_scalars$world_vsly_value_total)` trillion, equivalent to `r fmt_pct_income(econ_scalars$world_vsly_share_total)` of aggregate national income across `r n_countries` countries. These estimates are consistent in magnitude and methodology with recent global analyses that have quantified the economic value of reducing avoidable mortality. Chang et al. [-@Chang2024ECValue] estimated that the total economic value of reducing avoidable mortality across all causes and countries was several multiples of global income, using a comparable income-elasticity transfer approach to derive country-specific VSL and VSLY values. Verguet et al. [-@Verguet2024ECValue] extended this framework to noncommunicable diseases and injuries specifically, demonstrating that the economic returns to NCD mortality reduction were concentrated in low-income and middle-income countries, where the gap between observed and achievable mortality is widest. Our findings align with this pattern: the intervention scenarios modelled here target precisely the conditions and populations identified in those analyses as offering the highest returns per dollar invested. That the economic value of averting CVD deaths through hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy alone represents a substantial share of total avertable NCD mortality value underscores the outsized role that cardiovascular risk-factor management plays in the broader economic case for NCD investment [@Chang2024ECValue; @Verguet2024ECValue].

## Relation to previous literature

Our findings are broadly consistent with, and extend, previous global and regional analyses. Kontis et al. [-@Kontis2019] projected the probability of achieving SDG target 3.4 (a one-third reduction in premature NCD mortality by 2030) and identified inadequate cardiovascular risk-factor control as a major barrier in most countries. The NCD Countdown analyses identified blood pressure management and statin therapy as among the most efficient interventions for reducing premature CVD mortality in low- and middle-income settings [@Watkins2022NCD2030; @Bennett2020NCD2030Path]. Our study complements this work by providing country-specific projections over a 25-year horizon, enabling direct comparison of the relative contribution of each intervention. The NCD Countdown 2025 benchmarking analysis further documented the widening gap in CVD mortality trends between high-income and low-income countries [@NCDCountdown2025BenchmarkingProgress], lending additional urgency to the scale-up modelled here.

The Ford et al. analysis of the decline in US coronary mortality attributed approximately half of the observed reduction to evidence-based treatments, including statins and antihypertensives, and the remainder to risk-factor improvements [@Ford2007]. Similarly, Critchley et al. [-@Critchley2004] demonstrated that unfavourable risk-factor trends could offset treatment gains in rapidly developing countries. Our projections implicitly capture this tension by holding baseline risk-factor levels constant in the BAU scenario: the modelled health gains represent the incremental benefit of treatment scale-up above current trajectories.

## Strengths

This study has several notable strengths. First, it offers truly global coverage, incorporating country-specific epidemiological and demographic inputs for `r n_countries` countries rather than relying on regional aggregates. Second, the model explicitly captures the interaction between hypertension control and statin therapy using a multiplicative framework, thereby avoiding the upward bias inherent in additive effect assumptions. Third, by drawing on GBD 2023 estimates, WHO Global Health Estimates, and UNWPP 2024 population projections, the analysis reflects the latest and most robust sources of global health and demographic data. Fourth, treatment effects are appropriately de-duplicated: only gains attributable to incremental coverage beyond baseline practice are counted, preventing double-counting of existing intervention benefits. Finally, the 25-year projection horizon allows the model to account for the cumulative impact of sustained reductions in key risk factors --- effects that shorter-term analyses would fail to capture.

## Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. First, formal probabilistic sensitivity analysis was not conducted; results represent central estimates and do not incorporate uncertainty intervals from GBD inputs, meta-analytic effect sizes, or demographic projections. Second, the model assumes a static blood pressure distribution within countries --- no secular trends in population blood pressure and no endogenous updating as treatment coverage increases --- which may overestimate baseline risk in countries experiencing favourable risk-factor trends. Third, full adherence was assumed for hypertension therapy, and adherence-adjusted estimates for statin therapy may still exceed real-world levels in settings with limited health system capacity [@Li2024HyperlipidemiaMedicinesAccess; @Reith2026StatinAdverseEffects; @Baigent2010IntensiveLDLLowering]. Fourth, the linear scale-up assumption (2026--2030) is a simplification; actual programme expansion may follow non-linear trajectories with initial delays and subsequent acceleration. Fifth, no explicit health-system capacity constraints were modelled, meaning that the scenarios represent technical potential rather than implementation-ready projections. Sixth, COVID-19 excess mortality was modelled only for 2020--2021, and potential long-term cardiovascular sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection were not incorporated. Finally, the model does not capture potential interactions between interventions and other concurrent NCD prevention strategies, such as dietary sodium reduction or trans-fat elimination, which may modify the marginal benefit of hypertension control and statin therapy.

# Conclusion

Simultaneous achievement of WHO targets for hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy by 2030 was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_all)` million cardiovascular deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs across `r n_countries` countries between 2026 and 2050 --- gains concentrated precisely where they are needed most, in the countries and populations furthest from the targets today. Blood pressure control and statin therapy are not competing claims on a constrained prevention budget; they act on partially independent causal pathways, and pursuing both together produces more than either can deliver alone. The WHO HEARTS technical package provides the operational framework through which this integrated delivery is already happening --- by 2024, more than 22 million people with hypertension were being managed through HEARTS-based protocols in 38 low-income and middle-income countries, and Moran and colleagues have demonstrated that statin prescribing can be incorporated into those same workflows without requiring lipid laboratory capacity [@Moran2024; @Banigbe2025]. Scaling HEARTS to cover the full eligible population in the highest-burden settings and embedding both antihypertensive and lipid-lowering therapy within a single, standardised primary care encounter is the operational translation of what this study's combined scenario describes in aggregate. The projections presented here define a ceiling, not a forecast: they describe what these targets would yield under idealised conditions, and the distance between that ceiling and what current health system trajectories will actually produce is itself a measure of how much the implementation gap costs in human lives.

# Tables

**Table 1.** Cumulative CVD deaths averted by intervention scenario, `r study_years`.

```{r table1-paper, echo=FALSE}
tab1 <- copy(dt_cumul)[intervention %in% int_order]
setDT(tab1)
tab1[, intervention := factor(intervention, levels = int_order)]
setorder(tab1, intervention)

tab1_display <- tab1[, .(
  Intervention = intervention,
  `Deaths averted (millions)` = fmt_m(deaths_delayed),
  `Average per year (thousands)` = fmt_k(deaths_delayed / 25),
  `% of BAU deaths` = paste0(round(deaths_delayed / bau_total_deaths * 100, 1), "%")
)]

kable(tab1_display, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

*Note: Deaths averted = cumulative difference between business-as-usual and intervention scenario, 2026-2050. All four CVD causes combined: ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, hypertensive heart disease.*

**Table 2.** Cumulative CVD deaths averted by intervention scenario and cause of death (millions), `r study_years`.

```{r table2-paper, echo=FALSE}
setDT(dt_cause)
dt_cause[, cause_lbl := fcase(
  cause == "ihd",     "IHD",
  cause == "istroke", "Ischaemic stroke",
  cause == "hstroke", "Haemorrhagic stroke",
  cause == "hhd",     "Hypertensive HD",
  default = cause
)]

dt_t2_wide <- dcast(dt_cause[intervention %in% int_order],
                     intervention ~ cause_lbl,
                     value.var = "deaths_delayed", fill = NA)
dt_t2_wide[, intervention := factor(intervention, levels = int_order)]
setorder(dt_t2_wide, intervention)

cause_cols_display <- setdiff(names(dt_t2_wide), "intervention")
for (col in cause_cols_display) {
  dt_t2_wide[, (col) := fifelse(
    is.na(get(col)), "\u2013",
    fmt_m(get(col), digits = 2)
  )]
}

kable(dt_t2_wide, col.names = c("Intervention", cause_cols_display),
      align = c("l", rep("r", length(cause_cols_display))))
```

*Note: Values in millions. \u2013 = intervention does not affect this cause. Statin effects restricted to IHD and ischaemic stroke.*

  )]

  kable(econ_display, align = c("l", "r", "r"))
} else {

}

### Multi-State Transition Model {#sec:transition-model}

The model comprises three mutually exclusive health states for each cause $c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{ischaemic stroke}, \text{haemorrhagic stroke}, \text{HHD}\}$:

- **Well** ($W_{a,s,c,t}$): Disease-free individuals at risk of developing cause $c$
- **Sick** ($K_{a,s,c,t}$): Individuals living with prevalent disease $c$
- **Dead** ($D_{a,s,c,t}$): Individuals who have died from cause $c$

Individuals transition between states according to cause-specific incidence rates ($IR$: Well $\to$ Sick), case fatality rates ($CF$: Sick $\to$ Dead), and background mortality ($BG.mx$: exits from Sick; $BG.mx.all$: all-cause mortality applied to the total population). The four causes are modelled jointly but independently within each country--age--sex stratum; population-level accounting is maintained through all-cause mortality applied to the total population.

The model operates in discrete annual time steps with simultaneous age advancement: at each step, individuals at age $a$ in year $t$ advance to age $a+1$ in year $t+1$. New cohorts enter at age 20 each year. The projection period runs from 2017 (calibration start) through 2050.

**State transition equations.** For each location $\ell$, sex $s$, cause $c$, at age $a$ in year $t$, the state occupancies at age $a+1$ in year $t+1$ are:

*New cases:*

$$\text{NewCases}_{a+1,s,c,t+1} = W_{a,s,c,t} \times IR_{a,s,c,t} \times \varepsilon_{IR}(a,s,c,t)$$

*Sick population:*

$$K_{a+1,s,c,t+1} = K_{a,s,c,t} \times \left[1 - CF_{a,s,c,t} \times \varepsilon_{CF}(a,s,c,t) - BG.mx_{a,s,c,t} - covid.mx_{a,s,t}\right] + W_{a,s,c,t} \times IR_{a,s,c,t} \times \varepsilon_{IR}(a,s,c,t)$$

*Disease-specific deaths:*

$$D_{a+1,s,c,t+1} = K_{a,s,c,t} \times CF_{a,s,c,t} \times \varepsilon_{CF}(a,s,c,t)$$

*Total population (updated from external demographic projection):*

$$N_{a+1,s,t+1} = N_{a,s,t} - ALL.mx_{a,s,t}$$

*All-cause mortality:*

$$ALL.mx_{a,s,t} = \sum_c D_{a+1,s,c,t+1} + N_{a+1,s,t+1} \times \left(BG.mx.all_{a,s,t} + covid.mx_{a,s,t}\right)$$

*Well population (computed as residual):*

$$W_{a+1,s,c,t+1} = N_{a+1,s,t+1} - ALL.mx_{a+1,s,t+1} - K_{a+1,s,c,t+1}$$

where $\varepsilon_{IR}$ and $\varepsilon_{CF}$ are the multiplicative effect ratios from the intervention modules (equal to 1 under the business-as-usual scenario). COVID-19 excess mortality ($covid.mx$) is applied only for 2020--2021. All state occupancies are bounded below at zero, and transition rates are capped: $CF \leq 0.99$, $IR \leq 0.99$.

**Initial conditions.** At the model start year (2017) and for each new cohort entering at age 20:

$$K_{20,s,c,t_0} = N_{20,s,c,t_0} \times PREV_{20,s,c}$$

$$D_{20,s,c,t_0} = N_{20,s,c,t_0} \times DIS.mx_{20,s,c}$$

$$W_{20,s,c,t_0} = N_{20,s,c,t_0} \times \left(1 - PREV_{20,s,c} - BG.mx_{20,s,c}\right)$$

**Intervention combination.** When multiple interventions are applied simultaneously, their effect ratios combine multiplicatively:

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{total}}(a,s,c,t) = \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}}(a,s,c,t) \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP,DM}}(a,s,c,t) \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{statin}}(a,s,c,t)$$

$$\varepsilon_{CF,\text{total}}(a,s,c,t) = \varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP}}(a,s,c,t) \times \varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP,DM}}(a,s,c,t) \times \varepsilon_{CF,\text{statin}}(a,s,c,t)$$

Each intervention effect ratio defaults to 1 when the intervention is not active, so single-intervention and combined scenarios use the same multiplicative framework.

**Primary outcome.** Cumulative CVD deaths averted over the study period are computed as:

$$\text{Deaths averted} = \sum_{a,s,c,t} D^{\text{BAU}}_{a,s,c,t} - \sum_{a,s,c,t} D^{\text{intervention}}_{a,s,c,t}$$

(Parameter values for all transition rates are listed in the Key Parameter Appendix.)

### Hypertension Control Intervention Model {#sec:htn-model}

The hypertension control intervention modifies incidence and case fatality rates through a multi-step pipeline that integrates blood pressure distributions, GBD relative risks, Ettehad trial effect sizes, and linear coverage scale-up. Only *incremental* coverage above country-specific baseline control is credited with new effects, preventing double-counting of existing treatment benefits.

**Coverage scale-up.** Treatment coverage increases linearly from baseline to target over a specified period. The incremental coverage target above baseline is:

$$\Delta C_{\text{target}} = \max(C_{\text{target}} - C_{\text{baseline}}, 0)$$

The time-varying incremental coverage is:

$$\Delta C(t) = \Delta C_{\text{target}} \times \min\left(\frac{t - T_{\text{start}} + 1}{T_{\text{end}} - T_{\text{start}} + 1},\; 1\right)$$

with boundary conditions: $\Delta C(t) = 0$ for $t < T_{\text{start}}$ and $\Delta C(t) = \Delta C_{\text{target}}$ for $t > T_{\text{end}}$.

Coverage is applied only to hypertensive blood pressure bins ($\geq$ 140 mmHg). For hypertensive bins: $C_0 = C_{\text{baseline}}$ and $C_t(t) = C_{\text{baseline}} + \Delta C(t)$. For non-hypertensive bins ($<$ 140 mmHg): $C_0 = C_t = 0$.

**Step 1: Baseline blood pressure distribution.** The untreated population distribution across eight BP bins ($<$120, 120--129, ..., 180+) is obtained for each age--sex--location stratum: $P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}} \mid a, s, \ell)$.

**Step 2: Bin-specific baseline incidence via GBD relative risks.** GBD relative risks per 10 mmHg SBP increase above the reference ($<$120 mmHg) are applied as a power function of the distance from reference:

$$RR_{\text{GBD}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, a, c) = RR_{\text{per10}}^{(\text{SBP}_{\text{mid}} - 120)/10}$$

where $\text{SBP}_{\text{mid}}$ is the midpoint of the BP bin. A normalisation factor anchors bin-level rates to the overall incidence:

$$\alpha_{a,s,c,t} = \sum_{\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}} P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) \times RR_{\text{GBD}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, a, c)$$

Bin-specific incidence is then:

$$IR_{\text{bin}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) = \frac{RR_{\text{GBD}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, a, c) \times IR_{a,s,c,t}}{\alpha_{a,s,c,t}}$$

**Step 3: Diabetes-weighted Ettehad trial effect sizes.** The cumulative BP-reduction effect size for each bin and cause is computed as a diabetes-prevalence-weighted average of Ettehad trial estimates:

$$E_{\text{trial}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, c) = (1 - w_{\text{DM}}) \times E_{\text{noDM}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, c) + w_{\text{DM}} \times E_{\text{DM}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, c)$$

where $w_{\text{DM}}$ is the country-specific diabetes prevalence and $E_{\text{noDM}}$, $E_{\text{DM}}$ are cumulative bin-specific effect sizes from the Ettehad meta-analysis for non-diabetic and diabetic populations respectively.

**Step 4--5: Coverage-adjusted effect sizes.** The trial effect size is adjusted by the incremental coverage above baseline:

$$E_{\text{adj}}(t) = \frac{E_{\text{trial}} \times (C_t(t) - C_0)}{1 - E_{\text{trial}} \times C_0}$$

When $C_0 = 0$ (no prior treatment), this simplifies to $E_{\text{adj}}(t) = E_{\text{trial}} \times C_t(t)$.

**Step 6: New bin-specific incidence.**

$$IR_{\text{bin,new}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, t) = IR_{\text{bin}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) \times \left[1 - E_{\text{adj}}(t, \text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, c)\right]$$

**Step 7: Population-weighted aggregate incidence.**

$$IR_{\text{new}}(a, s, c, t) = \sum_{\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}} IR_{\text{bin,new}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, t) \times P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}})$$

**Step 8: Incidence effect ratio.**

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}}(a, s, c, t) = \frac{IR_{\text{new}}(a, s, c, t)}{IR_{\text{original}}(a, s, c, t)}$$

Values of $\varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}} < 1$ indicate reductions in disease incidence attributable to the intervention.

**Step 9: Case-fatality effect ratio.** Case fatality reductions are computed from the *incremental* aggregate coverage across hypertensive bins, preventing double-counting of baseline treatment effects:

$$\Delta C_{\text{delta}}(t, \text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) = \max\left(C_t(t) - C_0, 0\right)$$

$$C_{\text{agg}}^{\Delta}(a, s, c, t) = \frac{\sum_{\text{BP}_{\text{cat}} \in \text{HTN}} \Delta C_{\text{delta}}(t, \text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) \times P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}})}{\sum_{\text{BP}_{\text{cat}} \in \text{HTN}} P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}})}$$

where the summation is restricted to hypertensive bins (BP $\geq$ 140 mmHg). The case-fatality effect ratio is:

$$\varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP}}(a, s, c, t) = 1 - \rho_{CF,c} \times C_{\text{agg}}^{\Delta}(a, s, c, t)$$

where the cause-specific CF reduction factors are: $\rho_{CF,\text{IHD}} = 0.24$, $\rho_{CF,\text{IS}} = 0.36$, $\rho_{CF,\text{HS}} = 0.76$, $\rho_{CF,\text{HHD}} = 0.20$.

**Step 10.** The final output collapses across BP bins, retaining only the aggregate $IR_{\text{new}}$, $CF_{\text{new}}$, $\varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}}$, and $\varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP}}$ per age--sex--cause--year stratum.

(See Multi-State Transition Model for the baseline transition structure into which these effect ratios enter; see Key Parameter Appendix for all intervention effect sizes and their sources.)

#### Diabetes Component {#sec:htn-diabetes}

The diabetes-specific hypertension control intervention applies the same pipeline as the general-population intervention with three key modifications:

1. **Coverage target**: $C_{\text{target,DM}} = 0.80$ (versus 0.50 in the general population), corresponding to the Global Diabetes Compact target of 80% blood pressure control among people with diagnosed diabetes.

2. **Diabetes weighting**: The Ettehad effect sizes are computed with $w_{\text{DM}} = 1$ (full diabetes-specific effects), rather than the country-specific diabetes prevalence weight used in the general-population intervention.

3. **Population downscaling**: Because the intervention targets only the diabetic subpopulation, the effect is downscaled by the proportion of the population with diabetes ($d_{a,s,\ell}$) and raised blood pressure ($\phi_{\text{hyp}}$):

*Incidence:*

$$IR_{\text{bin,new}} = IR_{\text{bin}} \times \left(1 - d_{a,s,\ell} \times E_{\text{adj,DM}}(t)\right)$$

*Effect ratio blending (population-level):*

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP,DM}} = 1 \times (1 - d_{a,s,\ell} \times \phi_{\text{hyp}}) + \varepsilon_{IR,\text{raw}} \times d_{a,s,\ell} \times \phi_{\text{hyp}}$$

This ensures that the diabetes-specific intervention affects only the diabetic hypertensive fraction of the population, with the remainder retaining the baseline (unmodified) transition rate.

*Case fatality* is similarly downscaled: the incremental coverage delta is multiplied by the diabetes prevalence before aggregation, so that CF reductions apply only to the diabetic fraction:

$$\Delta C_{\text{delta,DM}} = d_{a,s,\ell} \times \max(C_t - C_0, 0)$$

The same CF reduction factors ($\rho_{CF,c}$) are applied to this diabetes-adjusted aggregate coverage.

(See Hypertension Control Intervention Model above for the general-population coverage scale-up structure, which shares the same functional form.)

### Statin Therapy Intervention Model {#sec:statin-model}

The statin intervention models the impact of scaling up lipid-lowering therapy among adults, with effects restricted to IHD and ischaemic stroke for ages $\geq 40$ years. The implementation: (i) scales up *incremental* coverage above country-specific baseline (to avoid double-counting), (ii) applies attributable fractions ($AF_{c,\ell}$) only for incidence effects (primary prevention), and (iii) applies trial-based relative risks directly for case fatality effects (secondary prevention), with ischaemic stroke CF effects restricted to the atherosclerotic fraction.

**Eligibility.** Statin effects are applied only to individuals aged $a \geq 40$ and for causes $c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{ischaemic stroke}\}$. For ages $a < 40$ or other causes, the effect ratios are set to 1 (no effect).

**Coverage scale-up.** The same linear scale-up function is used as for hypertension control (see Hypertension Control Intervention Model). Let $U_{0,\ell}$ denote baseline statin coverage at $T_{\text{stat,start}}$. The incremental target is:

$$\Delta U_{\text{target},\ell} = \max(U_{\text{target}} - U_{0,\ell},\; 0)$$

The time-varying incremental coverage above baseline is:

$$\Delta U(t, \ell) = \Delta U_{\text{target},\ell} \times \min\left(\frac{t - T_{\text{stat,start}} + 1}{T_{\text{stat,end}} - T_{\text{stat,start}} + 1},\; 1\right)$$

with $\Delta U(t,\ell) = 0$ for $t < T_{\text{stat,start}}$ and $\Delta U(t,\ell) = \Delta U_{\text{target},\ell}$ for $t > T_{\text{stat,end}}$.

**Trial-based relative risks and risk reductions.** Per approximately 1 mmol/L LDL-C reduction:

| Cause | $RR^{IR}_c$ | $RR^{CF}_c$ | $\delta^{IR}_c = 1 - RR^{IR}_c$ | $\delta^{CF}_c = 1 - RR^{CF}_c$ |
|-------|------------|------------|------|------|
| IHD | 0.74 | 0.80 | 0.26 | 0.20 |
| Ischaemic stroke | 0.80 | 0.96 | 0.20 | 0.04 |

Table: Statin relative risks from the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration [@Fulcher2015]

**Incidence effect size.** For $c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{ischaemic stroke}\}$ and $a \geq 40$, the incidence effect size incorporates the cause- and location-specific attributable fraction and a baseline-coverage adjustment in the denominator:

$$E^{IR}_{c,\ell}(t) = \frac{AF_{c,\ell} \times \delta^{IR}_c \times \Delta U(t,\ell) \times \alpha_{IR}}{1 - \delta^{IR}_c \times U_{0,\ell} \times \alpha_{IR}}$$

where $AF_{c,\ell}$ is the attributable fraction from GBD 2021 (default values: $AF_{\text{IHD}} = 0.15$, $AF_{\text{IS}} = 0.12$; country-specific values used where available) and $\alpha_{IR}$ is adherence for primary prevention (default: 1.0).

**Case fatality effect size.** CF effects are modelled directly from trial relative risks without attributable fractions. For ischaemic stroke, only the atherosclerotic fraction contributes:

$$E^{CF}_{c,\ell}(t) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\delta^{CF}_{\text{IHD}} \times \Delta U(t,\ell) \times \alpha_{CF}}{1 - \delta^{CF}_{\text{IHD}} \times U_{0,\ell} \times \alpha_{CF}} & \text{if } c = \text{IHD} \\[1em] \dfrac{\psi_{\text{athero}} \times \delta^{CF}_{\text{IS}} \times \Delta U(t,\ell) \times \alpha_{CF}}{1 - \delta^{CF}_{\text{IS}} \times U_{0,\ell} \times \alpha_{CF}} & \text{if } c = \text{ischaemic stroke} \end{cases}$$

where $\psi_{\text{athero}} = 0.60$ and $\alpha_{CF}$ is adherence for secondary prevention (default: 1.0).

**Modified rates.** For ages $a \geq 40$ and $c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{ischaemic stroke}\}$:

$$IR_{\text{new}}(a,s,c,t) = IR(a,s,c,t) \times \left[1 - E^{IR}_{c,\ell}(t)\right]$$

$$CF_{\text{new}}(a,s,c,t) = CF(a,s,c,t) \times \left[1 - E^{CF}_{c,\ell}(t)\right]$$

**Statin effect ratios:**

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{statin}}(a,s,c,t) = \begin{cases} 1 - E^{IR}_{c,\ell}(t) & \text{if } a \geq 40 \text{ and } c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{IS}\} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

$$\varepsilon_{CF,\text{statin}}(a,s,c,t) = \begin{cases} 1 - E^{CF}_{c,\ell}(t) & \text{if } a \geq 40 \text{ and } c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{IS}\} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

**Combined intervention effect.** When statin and hypertension control interventions are applied simultaneously, their effect ratios combine multiplicatively (see Multi-State Transition Model):

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{total}} = \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}} \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP,DM}} \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{statin}}$$

$$\varepsilon_{CF,\text{total}} = \varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP}} \times \varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP,DM}} \times \varepsilon_{CF,\text{statin}}$$

This multiplicative structure means the combined benefit exceeds the sum of individual effects, reflecting the partially independent causal pathways through which blood pressure control and lipid lowering reduce cardiovascular risk.

(See Key Parameter Appendix for all statin effect sizes and their sources.)

### DALY Calculation Methods {#sec:daly-methods}

Burden of disease was quantified using disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), computed as the sum of years of life lost due to premature mortality (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD). No age weighting or time discounting was applied. All computations were performed separately by age $a$, sex $s$, cause $c$, year $t$, location $\ell$, and intervention scenario $j$.

#### Years of Life Lost (YLL)

YLLs were computed as the product of the number of disease-specific deaths and the remaining life expectancy at the age of death:

$$YLL_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} = D_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} \times e_x(a, t, \ell)$$

where $D_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j}$ is the number of CVD deaths from cause $c$ (the `dead` variable from the state-transition model output) and $e_x(a, t, \ell)$ is the remaining life expectancy at exact age $a$ in year $t$ for location $\ell$, taken from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 revision, medium variant (both sexes combined). Life expectancy values are country- and year-specific, reflecting projected demographic conditions rather than a fixed global standard.

#### Years Lived with Disability (YLD)

YLDs were computed using a prevalence-based approach as the product of the number of prevalent CVD cases and a cause- and location-specific disability weight:

$$YLD_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} = K_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} \times DW_{c,\ell}$$

where $K_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j}$ is the number of individuals in the Sick (prevalent) state for cause $c$ from the state-transition model output, and $DW_{c,\ell}$ is the disability weight for cause $c$ in location $\ell$. Disability weights were derived from GBD 2023 data as the ratio of cause-specific years lived with disability to prevalence for each cause and location:

$$DW_{c,\ell} = \frac{YLD^{\text{GBD}}_{c,\ell}}{Prevalence^{\text{GBD}}_{c,\ell}}$$

This approach yields an implicit, frequency-weighted average disability weight that reflects the severity distribution observed in each country. No explicit duration of disability was modelled; the prevalence-based formulation captures the YLD burden attributable to the stock of prevalent cases at each time point.

#### Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALY)

Total DALYs were computed as:

$$DALY_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} = YLL_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} + YLD_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j}$$

DALYs averted were computed as the difference between the business-as-usual (BAU) scenario and each intervention scenario, summed across all strata:

$$\text{DALYs averted}_j = \sum_{a,s,c,t,\ell} DALY^{\text{BAU}}_{a,s,c,t,\ell} - \sum_{a,s,c,t,\ell} DALY^{j}_{a,s,c,t,\ell}$$

The same differencing logic was applied separately to YLLs averted and YLDs averted.

#### Reference Standards and Weights

### Economic Valuation Methods {#sec:econ-methods}

The economic value of avoided CVD mortality was estimated using the Value of a Statistical Life (VSL) and Value of a Statistical Life Year (VSLY) frameworks, following the benefit-transfer methodology of Robinson et al. [-@Robinson2019VSL].

#### Value of a Statistical Life (VSL) Transfer

Country-specific VSL was derived by transferring from a United States reference value using an income-elasticity adjustment:

$$\text{VSL}_{\ell,t} = \lambda \cdot Y^{\text{US}}_t \cdot \left(\frac{Y_{\ell,t}}{Y^{\text{US}}_t}\right)^{\eta}$$

where $\lambda = 160$ is the VSL-to-income ratio for the United States (such that $\text{VSL}_{\text{US}} = \lambda \cdot Y^{\text{US}}$), $Y_{\ell,t}$ is gross national income (GNI) per capita in purchasing power parity (PPP) terms for location $\ell$ in year $t$, $Y^{\text{US}}_t$ is the corresponding US GNI per capita, and $\eta$ is the income elasticity of VSL.

The primary estimate uses the differential elasticity recommended by Robinson et al. [-@Robinson2019VSL]:

$$\eta = \begin{cases} 0.8 & \text{if } Y_{\ell,t} \ge Y^{\text{US}}_t \\ 1.2 & \text{if } Y_{\ell,t} < Y^{\text{US}}_t \end{cases}$$

Sensitivity analyses used uniform elasticities of 1.0 and 1.5.

A floor constraint ensures that VSL does not fall below a minimum ratio to national income:

$$\text{VSL}_{\ell,t} = \max\!\left(\text{VSL}_{\ell,t},\; \phi \cdot Y_{\ell,t}\right)$$

where $\phi = 20$ is the minimum VSL-to-GNI ratio.

#### GNI Per Capita Projection

Observed GNI per capita (PPP, constant international dollars) was obtained from World Bank data. For years beyond the last observed value, GNI was projected forward using annual GDP per capita growth rates from the SSP2 scenario (IIASA SSP 3.1):

$$Y_{\ell,t} = Y_{\ell,t_0} \cdot \prod_{j=t_0+1}^{t} \left(1 + g_{\ell,j}^{\text{SSP2}}\right)$$

where $t_0$ is the last year with observed GNI and $g_{\ell,j}^{\text{SSP2}}$ is the SSP2 GDP per capita growth rate for year $j$, obtained by log-linear interpolation of five-year SSP nodes. This approach preserves observed GNI levels and applies only SSP-implied growth trajectories. A known limitation is that SSP projections provide GDP, not GNI, per capita; these series track closely for most countries but may diverge in economies with large net foreign income flows.

#### Value of a Statistical Life Year (VSLY)

A constant VSLY was derived by dividing the VSL by remaining life expectancy at the population-weighted average adult age:

$$\text{VSLY}_{\ell,t} = \frac{\text{VSL}_{\ell,t}}{\bar{e}_{\ell,t}}$$

where $\bar{e}_{\ell,t}$ is the undiscounted remaining life expectancy at the average age of the adult population ($\geq 20$ years) in location $\ell$ and year $t$, obtained from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 period life tables (both sexes combined). The average adult age was computed as:

$$\bar{a}_{\ell,t} = \frac{\sum_{a \geq 20} N_{a,\ell,t} \cdot a}{\sum_{a \geq 20} N_{a,\ell,t}}$$

where $N_{a,\ell,t}$ is the population at age $a$.

#### Life-Years Gained

The undiscounted life-years gained from avoided deaths were computed as:

$$\text{LYG}_{\ell,t,j} = \sum_{a} \Delta D_{a,\ell,t,j} \cdot e_x(a, t, \ell)$$

where $\Delta D_{a,\ell,t,j}$ is the number of deaths averted at age $a$ under intervention scenario $j$ (baseline minus intervention deaths) and $e_x(a, t, \ell)$ is the remaining life expectancy at exact age $a$ from WPP 2024 period life tables.

The VSLY-based monetary value of avoided mortality was then:

$$V^{\text{VSLY}}_{\ell,t,j} = \text{VSLY}_{\ell,t} \times \text{LYG}_{\ell,t,j}$$

Because the VSLY denominator uses life expectancy at the average adult age while the numerator uses age-specific life expectancy at the age of death, VSLY-based totals are not mechanically equal to VSL-based totals.

The VSL-based monetary value was computed directly as:

$$V^{\text{VSL}}_{\ell,t,j} = \text{VSL}_{\ell,t} \times \Delta D_{\ell,t,j}$$

where $\Delta D_{\ell,t,j} = \sum_a \Delta D_{a,\ell,t,j}$ is the total number of deaths averted.

#### Discounting

Annual monetary values were discounted to 2026 present value using calendar-year discount factors:

$$\delta_t = \frac{1}{(1 + r)^{t - 2026}}$$

where $r = 0.03$ (3%) for the primary analysis, with sensitivity analyses at $r = 0.01$ and $r = 0.05$. Discounted cumulative values were computed as:

$$V^{\text{disc}}_{\ell,j} = \sum_{t=2026}^{2050} \delta_t \cdot V_{\ell,t,j}$$

Results are also expressed as a share of discounted national income to facilitate cross-country comparison:

$$\text{Income share}_{\ell,j} = \frac{V^{\text{disc}}_{\ell,j}}{\sum_{t=2026}^{2050} \delta_t \cdot N_{\ell,t} \cdot Y_{\ell,t}}$$

where $N_{\ell,t}$ is total population and $Y_{\ell,t}$ is GNI per capita.
